articles.title: The firewall becomes the foothold: Attackers turn Check Point gateways against customers
articles.context: Attackers first gained access to the Mobile Access portal by exploiting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities
articles.full_text:
A firewall is intended to be a boundary attackers can’t cross.

But firewalls face the web, making them just as vulnerable to attack as other systems, as evidenced by the emergency hotfixes released by Check Point Software for several of its products. The patches address a high-severity privilege escalation flaw, CVE-2026-123039, that gives attackers root privilege access and the ability to send commands to the Gaia OS Dynamic CLI daemon, a core background process.

Hackers have been exploiting the 7.8-rated vulnerability since late October, and Check Point said “a couple of dozen” customers have been impacted.

Perhaps not surprisingly, adversaries gained initial access via PHP2Shell, the collective name for two critical PHP flaws tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The 9.2-severity-rated bugs allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE).

“For customers, one foothold delivered the full menu: Spying, staying, and destroying,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “For Check Point, the cost is trust. A firewall is supposed to be the strongest point in the network, not the softest.”

Granting unintended root access

CVE-2026-123039 is a bug in the Dynamic CLI IPC (Inter-Process Communication) interface which sends privileged command requests to the root-level Gaia OS Dynamic CLI. It is a local privilege escalation flaw, meaning an attacker already has to have local code execution ability on the appliance; this accounts for its 7.8 rating.

Attackers first gained access to the Mobile Access portal by exploiting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. They then escalated privileges to root using the CVE-2026-123039 zero-day exploits.

“Once attackers have root, they can run anything they like,” Dickson said. A management service on the appliance runs as root, listens on a local socket that any process on the box can write to, and never checks who is calling.

In this case, the attackers hid web shells inside the templates the portal uses to build its login page, and installed a TSGA backdoor and TSProxy malware that survives reboots, tucks itself into backups and snapshots, and hides inside the appliance’s own processes, he explained.

“That backdoor can copy the firewall configuration, which is essentially a blueprint of the network,” he said. It can also alter the firewall’s logs, concealing the attacker’s activities.

Check Point reported that, after gaining root access, the attackers then pivoted from the compromised gateway to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, deployed the destroy_v6 wiper, and left politically themed messages signed by a group calling itself Dream Security Ltd during the destructive stage.

Check Point advised security teams to immediately deploy the CVE-2026-123039 hotfixes, beginning with devices that expose Mobile Access to the internet. Those who can’t do so right away should stop the dynamic_server process and prevent it from restarting. However, they warned, this can come at the cost of some CLI commands.

Dickson also advised customers to turn off Mobile Access where it is not used, keep management interfaces off the internet entirely, and run the advisory’s log checks on any gateway exposed since late October, then cut the cord between the firewall and the hypervisor. A potentially exposed gateway should never have a trusted path into VMware ESXi.

They should also ship firewall logs off the box, as they happen, to a system the firewall cannot touch.

Products impacted by CVE-2026-123039 include Check Point’s Firewall, Multi-Domain Security Management Server, Security Gateway, Security Management Server, and Scalable Platforms.

Security tools are as big a target as what they protect

Once attackers have root access, the device basically becomes a trusted launching point for attacks against other systems that would otherwise stay protected, explained Erik Avakian, a technical counselor at Infotech. By effectively controlling the gateway, they can execute a wide array of nefarious actions.

The overall takeaway and irony of this, Avakian pointed out, is that the very technology organizations deploy to protect themselves can become one of their greatest vulnerabilities.

“Organizations can no longer assume their security infrastructure is inherently secure simply because it’s designed to provide protection,” he said. In reality, it is as much of a target as the systems it’s protecting.

Firewalls, VPN appliances, and security gateways are increasingly being targeted because they provide the greatest leverage and control, he noted. As such, security teams must treat these appliances as high value assets with the same access control safeguards, vulnerability management, monitoring, and incident response rigor applied to other critical infrastructure.

This means aggressively patching internet facing systems, restricting management access, monitoring for unusual administrative activity, and looking for indications of persistence or lateral movement, he said. But patches don’t evict already established attackers, so security teams must investigate and, where necessary, rebuild affected systems from trusted images.

And with AI accelerating attacks, CISOs should consider establishing a zero trust mindset and architecture collectively across the pillars of identity, network, applications, data, and devices, he said.

Keep an eye on the edge

Edge devices are primary targets, as they sit at the boundary, hold privileged access, and rarely get the endpoint monitoring that other systems do, noted Scott Miserendino, CTO at DataBee. Security appliances should be treated as the high-risk assets they’ve become.

In addition to patching and applying mitigations, he advised, defenders should assume there’s been a breach, hunting for published indicators of compromise (IOCs), routinely investigating network and endpoint security logs, and segmenting networks to reduce blast radius. “Security tools aren’t automatically secure, so defend the defenders,” he said.

And, Dickson pointed out, PHP2Shell will keep showing up because PHP sits underneath so much web software, including the portals bolted onto security appliances, so it should always be on defenders’ radar.

The management plane is a key target

Check Point is not alone as a victim of threat actors. Firewall management has become a favorite target for attackers across the industry.

In January, for instance, Fortinet disclosed that attackers abused its FortiCloud single sign-on to log into other customers’ FortiGate and FortiManager devices and create administrator accounts. In July and September, CISA added Check Point management server flaws to its catalog of exploited vulnerabilities.

That same month, the agency also added a Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center flaw, rated a perfect 10.0 in severity, that hands an unauthenticated attacker root access. And, in October, Palo Alto Networks warned of attacks on the PAN-OS management interface, again with “root on the firewall as the prize.”

“The logic is simple,” Dickson said: “The management plane holds the rulebook for the entire network.

Changing providers to one with fewer flaws is an option, but swapping vendors swaps one Achilles’ heel for another, he pointed out, as every vendor’s edge device has a web portal, and every web portal is a door. “The remedy is fewer doors,” he advised. “Shrink the internet-facing edge and put remote access behind one consistent identity policy.”

Ultimately, he noted, a firewall is not a wall, it is a computer sitting on the internet. “Attackers are treating it like one,” he said. “Security teams should defend it like one.”

articles.title: Check Point gateways hacked via PHP2Shell to deploy VMware ESXi wiper
articles.context: The attacker used PHP2Shell to gain access through the gateways’ Mobile Access portal, then exploited a newly disclosed zero-day vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-123039 to gain...
articles.full_text:
Vulnerable Check Point Security Gateway instances have been targeted in PHP2Shell attacks that deployed data-wiping malware on VMware ESXi hosts.

The attacks started on October 30, initially against Israeli organizations, and were conducted by an actor that ran the entire campaign, from initial access to lateral movement and launching PHP webshells.

In some instances, researchers found political messages during the destructive stage, raising questions about a possible false-flag operation.

PHP2Shell is the name for two critical PHP flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that allow unauthenticated remote code execution on vulnerable systems.

PHP fixed the vulnerabilities in emergency patches on October 21. However, according to Amazon Threat Intelligence, exploitation attempts started four days earlier.

CISA added both issues to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on October 26 and later warned that attackers were chaining PHP2Shell bugs with the Fragnesia Linux kernel flaw to gain root privileges.

Cybersecurity company Check Point says that the first exploitation wave targeted Israeli organizations, while a second one on November 2 affected companies in multiple countries and sectors.

The attacker used PHP2Shell to gain access through the gateways’ Mobile Access portal, then exploited a newly disclosed zero-day vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-123039 to gain root privileges.

Then they abused the privileges to install PHP webshells and the TSGA backdoor, which embeds a networking component called TSProxy to listen for attacker commands concealed within regular traffic.

In the attacks targeting Israeli organizations, the threat actors moved from the gateway to VMware ESXi hosts located using the gogo scanner, an open-source network reconnaissance tool.

In the last stage of the attack, the threat actor deployed a data wiper called destroy_v6 that recursively deletes data in the target directory.

The wiper first tries a zero fill to make recovery harder. It also supports a fast mode that skips the overwriting step.

Check Point also found that the attacker left on the ESXi host a note named DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt that references the ‘Dream Security Ltd.’

The note contains political messages and explicitly rejects ransom payment negotiations, indicating that the attackers’ sole goal is to cause damage and disruption.

Check Point tentatively linked TSGA and TSProxy to PhiliKit, a malware framework previously seen in attacks on Ivanti appliances and which ESET associated with the Chinese threat cluster UNC5221.

However, the attacks could not be attributed with confidence based on the available evidence.

According to the researchers, the second wave did not include the destructive activity, but the follow-on actions the threat actors took remain unclear.

Check Point recommends that customers install the November Jumbo Hotfix on all Management Servers and Security Gateways, prioritizing those with internet-facing Mobile Access portals.

The update addresses both PHP2Shell and the DynamicCLI privilege escalation flaw used in the attacks.

Administrators should also check for signs of compromise on previously exposed gateways, including session files containing upload_progress_pwn, unexpected CPconfigdaemon processes or binaries, and unexplained gaps in firewall logs.

Unauthorized SSH activity from the gateway to internal VMware ESXi hosts is also a clear sign of breach.

articles.title: Unpatched Check Point Gateways Are Being Wiped exploiting PHP2Shell
articles.context: “Following initial access, the attacker escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by exploiting CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege-escalation vulnerability in...
articles.full_text:
Unpatched Check Point gateways were hacked worldwide, leading to root access, backdoors, network intrusion and destructive wiper attacks.

Starting on 30 October, an attacker scanned and exploited Check Point Security Gateways that hadn’t been patched, going in through the Mobile Access portal. Check Point Research describes the activity as PHP2Shell for initial access, followed by a root-level privilege escalation tracked as CVE-2026-123039. The activity began about a week after a fix became available, from an IP address ending in 130.94.19[.]204.

“We have now confirmed that, in late October 2026, approximately one week after a security fix became available, activity originating from 130.94.19[.]204 targeted Israeli organizations through vulnerable Mobile Access portals on Check Point Security Gateways. Evidence suggested some cases of a successful compromise, with exploitation activity consistent with PHP2Shell, associated with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.” reads the report. “Following initial access, the attacker escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by exploiting CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege-escalation vulnerability in the DynamicCLI IPC interface. The attacker then used privileged command execution to deploy PHP webshells and establish persistence.”

There were two waves. The first, on 30 October, hit Israeli organizations, and some suffered destructive attacks. The second, on 2 November, reached organizations in several countries and sectors with no sign of destruction, and neither wave favored a particular sector. That points to opportunistic scanning, not careful targeting.

The first signs of the attack were PHP session files found in the /opt/CPcvpn-R81.20/tmp/ folder. These files contained a marker named upload_progress_pwn. The portal’s Apache and PHP processes also crashed hundreds of times, suggesting repeated attempts to exploit the vulnerability. The attacker then exploited another local flaw in the DynamicCLI interface to gain root privileges, giving them full control of the device.

With root access, the attackers installed PHP webshells in the folder used by the portal to create login pages. These files had names starting with zz and ending in .tpl. Initially, they contained simple tools for running commands. The attackers later replaced them with more advanced versions that required a hardcoded key, could execute system commands and PHP code, and supported file uploads. Uploaded files were first saved as /tmp/.up.tpl and then copied into the portal’s folder under the name challenge_render.tpl.

The attackers then installed a separate backdoor called TSGA, launched from /tmp/CPconfigdaemon. Running with root privileges, it moved itself, restarted under the name slot_CPconfigdaemon, and installed a second tool called TSProxy at /lib/libcpfwcommon.so. TSProxy was designed to run inside processes on the Check Point appliance and monitor network activity. It intercepted selected network connections used by the attackers while leaving normal network traffic unaffected.

TSGA is built for Check Point gear. It offers encrypted remote access, configuration theft, persistence through backups and snapshots, process injection and tampering with binary firewall logs. TSProxy adds encrypted proxying.

From the gateway, the attackers ran the gogo scanner to map the internal network, then moved over SSH to a VMware ESXi host using the vpxuser account. There they staged a Linux wiper, destroy_v6, and ran it. It deletes files in a target folder regardless of extension, overwrites them with zeros first unless run in fast mode, and can skip listed folders.

The wiper also leaves a note named DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt in each folder it processes. The note is politically themed, includes a timestamp, is written in Hebrew with reference to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, and rejects ransom talks. At least nobody has to haggle.

Attribution is more difficult. TSGA and TSProxy appear to be modified versions of PhiliKit, a framework previously found in attacks against Ivanti devices and linked by ESET to UNC5221, a China-linked threat group. The tools share several unique features with PhiliKit, including code, configuration settings and encryption details. These similarities include the use of TCP port 11072 and a Unix socket at /tmp/.p_sock. TSProxy also uses the same credentials, communication secrets, TLS certificate and private key as a PhiliKit component called libdssafe.so.

Other findings also suggest a possible connection to Chinese threat actors. The gogo network scanner has previously been associated with China-linked groups, while the attackers used LightNode VPS servers, a hosting provider also used by these actors. The scanning activity took place between 00:00 and 09:00 UTC, corresponding to normal working hours in China (08:00 to 17:00).

However, some aspects of the operation do not match UNC5221’s known activity and objectives. These include the destructive attacks, the focus on Israeli organizations, the Hebrew-language message left by the wiper and the malware name, which appears to reference the word “Philistine”.

Check Point says several explanations are possible. UNC5221 may have carried out the entire operation, or it may have provided initial access to another threat actor. The attackers could also have deliberately left clues to mislead investigators. Another possibility is that the destructive attacks were intended to hide a different objective.

The note uses the Dream Security brand, and Dream recently published research on PHP2Shell attacks on Palo Alto Networks devices by China-nexus actors. That timing raises the possibility of retaliation, but the evidence doesn’t establish a clear motive.

“Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation. Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation.” concludes the report. “It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

articles.title: Check Point warns of zero-day flaw exploited for root access
articles.context: In a separate report, Check Point said the attackers first gained access to the Mobile Access portal by exploiting the PHP2Shell vulnerability, then escalated privileges to root...
articles.full_text:
Check Point Software has released emergency hotfixes to address a high-severity flaw that hackers have been exploiting to gain root privileges and establish persistence on vulnerable devices since late October.

Tracked as CVE-2026-123039, this local privilege escalation vulnerability was found in the DynamicCLI IPC (Inter-Process Communication) interface used to send privileged command requests to the root-level Gaia OS DynamicCLI (dynamic_server) daemon.

"Check Point observed an active exploit of this vulnerability against a couple of dozen customers," the company warned in a Thursday security advisory.

"The Gaia OS DynamicCLI daemon runs as root and listens on a world-writable local socket (/tmp/dynamic_socket) without authenticating connecting processes. An authenticated local user can send a command to the socket and have it executed as root."

The list of Check Point products vulnerable to attacks exploiting the CVE-2026-123039 flaw includes the company's Firewall, Multi-Domain Security Management Server, Scalable Platforms, Security Gateway, and Security Management Server.

In a separate report, Check Point said the attackers first gained access to the Mobile Access portal by exploiting the PHP2Shell vulnerability, then escalated privileges to root using CVE-2026-123039 zero-day exploits.

Next, the threat actors dropped webshells and installed TSGA backdoor and TSProxy malware that was previously spotted while investigating attacks targeting Ivanti appliances, then pivoted from the compromised gateway to a VMware ESXi host and deployed destructive wiper malware.

Check Point advised security teams who can't immediately deploy the CVE-2026-123039 hotfixes to stop the dynamic_server process and prevent it from restarting as a temporary mitigation measure.

The company also shared indicators of compromise (IOCs), and it said that customers can find evidence of compromise by checking for commands commonly associated with exploitation attempts, the use of the system() sink (uncommon or absent in legitimate traffic), and commands that don't use the default Clish wrapper (indicating that it was executed as root through the socket and requires further investigation).

In September, Check Point warned customers that attackers had been exploiting two other critical Security Management Server (CVE-2026-93616) and Security Gateway (CVE-2026-85102) remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in zero-day attacks that didn't require privileges on the targeted systems.

Over the last two years, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added five Check Point flaws to its catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities, two of which have also been abused by ransomware gangs.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit PHP2Shell Flaws in Check Point Gateways to Deploy TSGA Backdoor and Wipe ESXi Files
articles.context: "The issue is a local privilege escalation and requires the attacker to already have local code execution on the appliance," Check Point said, adding it "observed an active...
articles.full_text:
An unknown threat actor has been observed targeting unpatched Check Point Security Gateways to obtain initial access via the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and then a previously unreported local privilege escalation flaw in Gaia OS to deploy a backdoor called TSGA.

The activity, detailed by Check Point, began on October 30, 2026, and targeted Israeli organizations, with a broader follow-up wave on November 2, 2026, that targeted organizations across multiple countries and sectors. Some of the organizations singled out in the first wave have also been at the receiving end of destructive actions that include the deployment of wiper malware.

"PHP2Shell provided initial access, followed by privilege escalation through the DynamicCLI interface, tracked as CVE-2026-123039," Check Point said. "The attackers then deployed PHP web shells, the persistent TSGA backdoor, and its embedded TSProxy networking component."

"The attackers pivoted from the gateway to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, deployed the destroy_v6 wiper, and left politically themed DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt notes during the destructive stage."

CVE-2026-123039 (CVSS score: 7.8) is a missing authorization flaw that could enable privilege escalation to root in the DynamicCLI process, enabling any authenticated local user to run arbitrary commands by writing a single request to the socket.

"The issue is a local privilege escalation and requires the attacker to already have local code execution on the appliance," Check Point said, adding it "observed an active exploit of this vulnerability against a couple of dozen customers."

The issue impacts versions R82.20, R82.10, R82, R81.20, R81.10, and R81 of the following products -

Check Point Force Firewalls

Check Point Management and Log Servers

Multi-Domain Security Management and Multi-Domain Log Server

Maestro Orchestrator

"In late October 2026, approximately one week after a security fix became available, activity originating from 130.94.19[.]204 targeted Israeli organizations through vulnerable Mobile Access portals on Check Point Security Gateways," Check Point said.

"Evidence suggested some cases of a successful compromise, with exploitation activity consistent with PHP2Shell, associated with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619."

After obtaining initial access, the unknown hacking group is said to have escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by weaponizing CVE-2026-123039 and deploying PHP web shells with an aim to establish persistent access. The web shells support command execution and file upload capabilities.

The November 2, 2026, wave is said to have targeted some Israeli organizations that had already been targeted in the first wave, alongside other organizations worldwide, without demonstrating any specific geographic or sector preference, indicating an opportunistic initial-access effort.

The access afforded by the web shell paves the way for TSGA, a standalone passive backdoor that also includes a second component called TSProxy. TSGA, deployed as slot_CPconfigdaemon, has been described as a Linux gateway implant with Check Point-specific functionality, offering encrypted remote access, configuration theft, backup and snapshot persistence, process injection, and binary firewall-log tampering.

"[TSProxy's] injection code loads this library into selected appliance processes, where it intercepts networking functions to handle specially marked attacker connections while allowing ordinary traffic to continue," Check Point said. "This combines a persistent standalone backdoor with concealed access through existing appliance services."

Some of the other post-exploitation actions observed are listed below -

Deploying the gogo scanner on the gateway to discover internal assets and services across the network.

Moving laterally to a VMware ESXi host over SSH by authenticating with the vpxuser service account.

Staging a Linux ELF wiper called destroy_v6 and executing it. The malware recursively traverses the target directory and deletes all files regardless of their extension. It also attempts to overwrite files with zeros before deleting them.

Dropping a note named "DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt" in each processed directory.

Both TSGA and TSProxy are assessed to be Check Point-specific components of a toolkit dubbed PhiliKit that was first documented by ESET in June 2026, attributing it to a China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221).

Other factors that point to the involvement of a possible China-aligned threat actor include the use of LightNode VPS infrastructure and the fact that scanning activity was concentrated between 12 and 9 a.m. UTC, coinciding with typical Chinese working hours.

However, the cybersecurity company said it does not have enough evidence to link the latest campaign to the threat actor or other known Chinese-nexus groups, citing the following reasons -

Use of wiper malware

Focus on Israel and explicit references to the Israeli-Palestine conflict in the wiper note

"Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation," Check Point said. "Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen."

articles.title: PHP2Shell Exploited in Destructive Check Point Gateway Attacks
articles.context: Threat actors have been exploiting PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to hack Check Point Gateway appliances and deploy a wiper against victim organizations, Check Point reports
articles.full_text:
Threat actors have been exploiting PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to hack Check Point Gateway appliances and deploy a wiper against victim organizations, Check Point reports.

The attacks unfolded in two waves. An initial, destructive round started on October 30 and targeted Israeli organizations, and a second one started on November 2, targeting organizations across multiple countries.

PHP2Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, refers to two critical vulnerabilities leading to remote code execution (RCE) and affecting all PHP versions from PHP 5 onwards. They were patched on October 21, but exploitation started days before patches and mass exploitation shortly after.

Dream has linked attacks targeting PHP2Shell to root Palo Alto Networks firewalls to Chinese hackers, and the hackers targeting Check Point gateways have left a note mentioning the cybersecurity firm.

As part of the Check Point campaign, the attackers exploited PHP2Shell for initial access, then targeted CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege escalation in the DynamicCLI process, to gain root access and deploy PHP webshells and establish persistence.

In late October, the attackers targeted Check Point Mobile Access gateways across multiple Israeli organizations. They placed PHP webshells in a directory the Mobile Access portal uses to construct login pages, allowing them to send commands and establish a stronger foothold on the environment.

Next, they deployed TSGA and TSProxy, variants of the malware framework PhiliKit previously seen (PDF) in China-linked UNC5221’s hacking into Ivanti products, for backdoor access and network function interception.

The attackers followed up with internal asset discovery, then moved laterally to a VMware ESXi host where they deployed and executed a wiper, and then deployed a note mentioning Dream Security.

According to Check Point, the hackers operated during typical Chinese working hours. Despite this and the use of China-linked malware and infrastructure, the use of a wiper and the destructive nature of the attacks do not align with known Chinese cyber operations.

“Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation. Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen,” Check Point says.

The second wave targeted Check Point Security Gateways across organizations worldwide, including some Israeli entities targeted in the first wave. No destructive activity was observed during this second wave.

“Neither wave showed a clear sector preference, suggesting opportunistic initial-access attempts rather than sector-specific targeting,” Check Point notes.

Customers can now choose anything from a scoped penetration test to an objective-based engagement. Each engagement shows three things: how an attacker could break into the environment, how far the attacker could get, and whether the security team would detect the attack. Every engagement answers three questions: how an attacker gets in, how far they get, and whether your team detects the attack.

Attackers move fast, and AI is making them faster. Attackers rarely need one critical flaw; they chain small weaknesses into a full attack path. Scans and checklist testing validate individual controls, but they don’t show how a determined attacker would move through an environment.

The extended penetration testing closes that gap. Check Point Research has identified active, in-the-wild exploitation of PHP2Shell, a vulnerability in PHP that also affects Check Point Security Gateways. In the observed incidents, the attacker exploited PHP2Shell to gain initial access, then used a local privilege escalation vulnerability to obtain root privileges and establish persistence.

Security fixes for Check Point Security Gateway and Management were available one week before the attack, on October 23rd. Only a couple of dozen unpatched systems, in a single region, were compromised in the observed incidents. Affected customers were notified in real time. Check Point Research, through its Incident Response teams, worked to remediate affected systems.

We recommend that customers install the November Jumbo Hotfix on all Management Servers and Security Gateways as soon as operationally possible.

Overview

As part of BLAST and our Frontier AI Readiness Program, Check Point continues to release monthly security fixes that include fixes for vulnerabilities and security hardening.

Recent security incidents, such as PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) and HTTP2Shell, also known as Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497), a Brotli decompression vulnerability affecting Node.js and other software, led us to release hotfixes that are now part of the November Jumbo Hotfix.

articles.title: PHP2Shell Exploitation on Check Point Gateway
articles.context: TSGA and TSProxy are modified variants of PhiliKit, a malware framework previously documented in attacks exploiting Ivanti vulnerabilities
articles.full_text:
Key findings

Beginning on 30 October 2026, an attacker executed scanning and exploitation activity against organizations with unpatched Check Point Security Gateways, using Mobile Access portals with PHP2Shell as initial access followed by CVE-2026-123039.

The first wave, on October 30, targeted Israeli organizations and included destructive activity against some of them. A broader second wave on November 2 targeted organizations across multiple countries and sectors, with no evidence of destructive activity

In the investigated intrusion, PHP2Shell provided initial access, followed by privilege escalation through the DynamicCLI interface, tracked as CVE-2026-123039. The attackers then deployed PHP webshells, the persistent TSGA backdoor and its embedded TSProxy networking component.

The attackers pivoted from the gateway to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, deployed the destroy_v6 wiper, and left politically themed DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt notes during the destructive stage.

TSGA and TSProxy are modified variants of PhiliKit, a malware framework previously documented in attacks exploiting Ivanti vulnerabilities. Both tools share distinctive code, configuration, and cryptographic material with the framework

Although ESET associated PhiliKit with China nexus UNC5221, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation. Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen.

The note left during the destructive activity uses the Dream Security brand. Dream had recently published research on PHP2Shell exploitation of Palo Alto Networks devices by China nexus actors. While this timing raises the possibility of retaliation, the available evidence does not establish a clear motive.

Introduction

We have now confirmed that, in late October 2026, approximately one week after a security fix became available, activity originating from 130.94.19[.]204 targeted Israeli organizations through vulnerable Mobile Access portals on Check Point Security Gateways. Evidence suggested some cases of a successful compromise, with exploitation activity consistent with PHP2Shell, associated with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

Following initial access, the attacker escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by exploiting CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege-escalation vulnerability in the DynamicCLI IPC interface. The attacker then used privileged command execution to deploy PHP webshells and establish persistence.

A second scanning wave on November 2nd targeted some Israeli organizations previously targeted during the first wave, alongside additional organizations worldwide, with no apparent focus on Israel. Neither wave showed a clear sector preference, suggesting opportunistic initial-access attempts rather than sector-specific targeting.

Infection Flow

On October 30, 2026, the first signs of exploitation appeared on the targeted Check Point Mobile Access gateways. PHP session artifacts were created under /opt/CPcvpn-R81.20/tmp/, including session files containing the upload_progress_pwn marker associated with the exploitation activity. During the same window, the portal’s Apache/PHP workers experienced hundreds of segmentation faults, providing additional evidence of repeated exploitation attempts against the service.

Figure 1 – Infection chain

After gaining access to the Mobile Access portal, the attackers escalated privileges to root by exploiting CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege-escalation vulnerability in the DynamicCLI interface. With privileged command execution, the attackers placed PHP webshells in <templates>, a directory used by the Mobile Access portal to construct its login pages. These webshells provide a way to send commands through the web portal, establishing a stronger foothold within the compromised environment.

printf <base64 Webshell> | base64 -d > <templates>/zz<random>.tpl

The attacker used multiple .tpl files with names matching the pattern zz*.tpl Each initially received a small command-execution shell, which was then replaced with a more capable version. The expanded shell requires the hardcoded key zz2026 and supports operating-system commands, PHP code execution, and file uploads. Uploaded files are saved to the fixed path /tmp/.up.tpl. The attackers subsequently issued commands to copy that file into the portal’s directory as challenge_render.tpl.

The attackers then moved from web-based access to a standalone passive backdoor, launching the TSGA malware (/tmp/CPconfigdaemon) in the background and redirecting its output to a hidden temporary log:

nohup /tmp/CPconfigdaemon >/tmp/.bd.log 2>&1 & printf started

When executed as root, the malware relocates itself and relaunches under the name slot_CPconfigdaemon in the boot persistence directory. The executable also carries a second component, TSProxy: an embedded shared library that it writes to /lib/libcpfwcommon.so. Its injection code loads this library into selected appliance processes, where it intercepts networking functions to handle specially marked attacker connections while allowing ordinary traffic to continue. This combines a persistent standalone backdoor with concealed access through existing appliance services.

The attackers then deployed the gogo scanner on the gateway to discover internal assets and services across the network and continued to move laterally to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, authenticating with the vpxuser service account. On the ESXi host, they staged the destroy_v6 wiper to /tmp/des wiper and executed it. Finally, the attackers left a note that accompanied the destructive activity named DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt.

Figure 2 – Destructive activity note

Technical Analysis

Webshells

The expanded PHP webshell requires a hardcoded key to access its command-execution, PHP-evaluation, and file-upload functions. It supports both plain-text and Base64-encoded, XOR-obfuscated commands, and saves uploaded files to /tmp/.up.tpl.

Figure 3 – Webshell code

Wiper

The Linux ELF wiper destroy_v6 accepts a target directory as a command-line argument. The optional -f flag enables fast deletion, while -w specifies a pipe-separated list of directories to exclude. The wiper recursively traverses the target directory, deleting files regardless of extension and skipping excluded subtrees. By default, it attempts to overwrite files with zeros before deleting them, fast mode skips the overwrite step. It also writes DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt to each processed directory. This politically themed note includes a timestamp and explicitly rejects ransom negotiations.

TSGA – slot_CPconfigdaemon

The TSGA implant, deployed as slot_CPconfigdaemon, is a Linux gateway implant with substantial Check Point-specific functionality. It provides encrypted remote access, configuration theft, backup and snapshot persistence, process injection, and binary firewall-log tampering.

TSProxy

TSProxy is a Linux shared-library backdoor embedded in TSGA and dropped as /lib/libcpfwcommon.so and supports encrypted SOCKS-style proxying.

Tools relationship

Both TSGA and TSProxy are Check Point-specific components linked to the previously reported PhiliKit-associated toolset. PhiliKit is a passive backdoor and installer targeting Ivanti VPN appliances and was previously reported following the February 25, 2026 upload of a sample named philistine to VirusTotal.

TSGA and the PhiliKit implant have roots in Tiny SHell, and share a core set of remote-control capabilities. Both implement authenticated, encrypted communications through TCP port 11072 and the Unix socket /tmp/.p_sock. The analyzed PhiliKit build restricts its TCP listener to loopback, whereas TSGA listens on all IPv4 interfaces. Both provide interactive shells with pseudo-terminal allocation, configurable terminal dimensions and bidirectional input/output. Operators can execute arbitrary shell commands and Python or Perl scripts, retrieve their output, transfer files using operator-selected paths, and collect selected or full appliance configurations over the encrypted channel.

TSProxy shares distinctive configuration with libdssafe.so, the networking component embedded in PhiliKit package: identical operator credentials, transport secrets, three matching activation-selector digests, and the same TLS certificate and private key. These overlaps strongly support a shared tooling lineage.

Attribution

The implants delivered to the gateway, TSGA and TSProxy are part of the PhiliKit malware family, which has been associated with the China-nexus group UNC5221 and previous exploitation of Ivanti appliances. In addition, gogo scanner has also been reported in connection with Chinese-nexus threat actors exploiting Ivanti vulnerabilities.

The infrastructure IP addresses used by the attacker were hosted on LightNode VPS infrastructure, a service previously associated with activity by Chinese- nexus threat actors.

The scanning activity was concentrated between 00:00 and 09:00 UTC, corresponding to 08:00–17:00 in China and broadly aligning with typical Chinese working hours.

With all the above, the following attributes that appeared in the described campaign do not appear to fully align with known Chinese-nexus groups (and specifically UNC5221) motives and interests:

Destructive operation

Focus on Israel and wiper note in Hebrew referring to the Israeli-Palestine conflict

Philikit name derived from the malware internal name philistine

Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation. Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen.

The federal, state, local government, and education sectors are under growing cyber pressure, and the attack surface is shifting to where they now serve citizens most. According to Check Point’s 2026 Cyber Security Report, government organizations faced an average of 2,680 cyber-attacks per organization each week in 2025, a 17% increase from 2024, making government the second most targeted sector worldwide. As government organizations move services online, deploy citizen self-service portals, connect APIs, and integrate AI into mission-critical workflows, every new capability creates a new entry point. A successful attack doesn’t just disrupt IT-it can interrupt essential services, expose sensitive citizen records, compromise internal secrets, and undermine public trust.

The data reflects that reality. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report recorded 3,634 public-sector incidents and 2,410 confirmed data disclosure breaches, with exploitation of vulnerabilities accounting for 40% of initial access, and personal data, internal data, and secrets among the most compromised. That makes runtime web application and API protection especially critical for government organizations running legacy systems, third-party applications, and public-facing services that cannot always be patched immediately.

Check Point has been addressing this risk inside government trust and compliance requirements since achieving FedRAMP Certification for its Check Point Platform for Government in 2025. Now Check Point is expanding its FedRAMP-Certified packages to include Check Point WAF, bringing prevention-first web application security, API protection, Bot mitigation, DDoS defence, CDN-integrated delivery, and GenAI application security into the same government-certified platform.

Security Built for Modern Government Applications

Government organizations no longer operate static websites. Today’s public sector runs digital citizen portals, API-driven benefit and payment systems, cloud-native applications, and AI-enabled interfaces that connect identity, records, contractors, and partner organizations across the public sector. This growing interconnection makes the application layer more dynamic, complex, and exposed.

AI is also transforming both the speed of attacks and the security model required to stop them. Frontier AI technologies demonstrate how vulnerabilities can be discovered and validated autonomously at unprecedented speed and scale. Attackers are already using AI-powered tools to generate payload variations and exploit weaknesses faster, making signature-based protection increasingly ineffective. As a result, pre-emptive, AI-driven prevention that can stop unknown attacks without signatures or emergency updates is becoming essential.

Modern Web Application and API Protection (WAAP) must secure far more than a single website or API endpoint. Government organizations need prevention-first protection across the entire application environment, including:

Pre-emptively prevent known, unknown, and zero-day web and API attacks before they reach the application

End-to-end API security with automated discovery, schema validation and authentication enforcement

Availability of critical services with strong bot mitigation and DDoS protection against automated abuse and disruption

Block GenAI application attacks including prompt injection, data leakage and harmful content

Simplify operations with centralized management that reduces tool sprawl and complexity across the full application stack

Check Point WAF brings all these capabilities into a single consolidated platform, purpose-built for the modern application reality that government organizations face today. By adding it to the FedRAMP certified packages, federal organizations can now secure public-facing applications and APIs through the same government-certified platform they already trust with the prevention, visibility, and control needed to protect modern application environments without adding complexity or managing separate tools for every risk.

Why This Matters Now

The public-sector application attack surface is expanding quickly as government organizations modernize services, expose more APIs, and begin adopting AI-enabled workflows. At the same time, AI is accelerating the speed at which attackers find and exploit those weaknesses.

According to Check Point 2026 Cloud Security Report, 70% of organizations run GenAI workloads in production, yet visibility has not kept up. Only 5% of organizations have full visibility into how AI is used, and just 14% actively enforce and audit an AI security policy.

PHP2Shell shows how fast the window closes. Two critical PHP flaws, each rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale, let an attacker run code on a server with one crafted request, with no password, account, or user interaction. Attacks started before the patch landed on October 21, 2026, and government organizations took sites offline to cope. Check Point WAF preemptively blocked PHP2Shell with no signature, rule, or configuration change.

This is why expanding Check Point’s FedRAMP certification packages to include Check Point WAF matters. It is not just another security product. It is a way to help public-sector organizations protect the applications, APIs, and digital services that citizens, employees, contractors, and partners depend on every day.

Available Through the FedRAMP Marketplace

Check Point is listed on the FedRAMP Marketplace, with Check Point WAF included in the certification, making it easier for federal mission owners to discover, evaluate, and procure the solution.

articles.full_text:
Branch Traffic Has Changed. Security Has to Follow.

A traditional branch was simple in nature: a location that connects back to headquarters where applications, data, and security controls were housed. Today the landscape is wildly different. A branch may connect directly to SaaS apps, clouds, data centers, the open internet, and other locations within the enterprise. And while all those connections are being made, often many at one time, employees expect video calls and cloud applications to perform just as well in the office as they do at home.

The branch itself has become more complex, too. Connected devices can range from printers and ‘smart building’ systems to specialized IoT equipment. Employees may also access AI applications and services directly from the network. And many branch locations are expected to manage all of this without dedicated security personnel on site.

Routing all that activity back through headquarters can introduce unnecessary latency and cost. However, without the right controls you’re opening yourself up to new exposure. The modern branch needs connectivity, protection, and resilience to work together.

Now is the Time for Connectivity to Adapt to the Application

Not every application needs the same network path.

Video calls? Highly sensitive to latency and packet loss. Large backup transfers? Often prioritize cost over speed. Internal business applications? Might need an encrypted route back to a data center.

Software-defined wide area networking (SD-WAN) gives organizations more control over those decisions because, rather than relying on one fixed route, SD-WAN can evaluate available connections and steer traffic based on the application, business policy, and real-time network conditions.

Multiple links can add another layer of resilience. If one connection degrades or fails, traffic can move to a healthier path automatically. But branch continuity depends on more than WAN alone. Firewall clustering and hardware redundancy can help keep both connectivity and protection available when individual components fail.

For businesses that depend on real-time transactions, voice and video, cloud apps, or always-on access to corporate resources, that resilience helps keep a local issue from becoming a larger business interruption.

See how Hybrid Mesh connects security across the distributed enterprise. Download Our CISO Guide

The Branch Has Become A Bigger Security Surface

Direct internet access improves performance, but it also changes where traffic needs to be inspected and protected. Branch firewalls increasingly need to secure traffic locally while supporting the same high-bandwidth applications they are helping accelerate.

And the risk now extends well beyond internet traffic: printers, cameras, building systems, medical devices, and industrial equipment can all expand the internal attack surface. Many of those devices were never designed with modern cybersecurity in mind, making visibility, segmentation, and threat prevention increasingly important inside the branch as well as at its perimeter.

And of course AI adds another consideration entirely. Employees may use third-party AI applications, agents, or connected tools directly from the branch. Security teams need visibility into that activity and the ability to apply policy, including controls that help prevent sensitive data from being shared through prompts. Meanwhile, attackers are using AI to accelerate and develop new exploits, malware, and phishing tools. Branch security therefore needs strong prevention at the point where traffic is already being inspected, rather than relying on another, additional layer.

Every Branch Should Be Easier to Operate

A distributed enterprise may have dozens, hundreds, or thousands of locations. Managing each branch as its own network creates complexity that grows exponentially with every new site that needs to fit within the existing architecture.

Centralized policy, zero-touch provisioning, network-health monitoring, and unified visibility can make branches easier to deploy and manage while keeping protection more consistent across locations.

That matters especially when there is no security specialist sitting at every branch. Centralized management allows teams to deploy and maintain protection across large numbers of sites without turning every new location, policy change, or connectivity issue into an on-site project.

Bring Connectivity and Security Together at the Branch

Hybrid Mesh Network Security connects the branch with the security architecture protecting data centers, clouds, applications, and users across the enterprise.

Check Point Firewall combines advanced threat prevention with Check Point SD-WAN to help organizations protect branch traffic while optimizing how applications connect. AI security at the firewall adds visibility and policy controls for employee AI usage, while centralized management and zero-touch deployment help maintain consistent protection across distributed locations.

Integration with Check Point SASE extends that approach beyond the branch, helping connect users and locations to the applications and resources they need while keeping branch security part of the broader enterprise architecture.

Organizations who prefer a hybrid security approach can benefit from a hybrid SASE deployment. This way, they can cater to remote users with cloud-based security (SSE) connected to on-prem SD WAN, and also protect office users through network firewalls embedded with SD WAN for optimized branch connectivity.

articles.full_text:
Key takeaways

Organizations experienced 2,550 weekly cyber attacks on average in October, down 9% month over month but up 32% year over year.

Education remained the most targeted sector, averaging 5,934 weekly attacks per organization, a 33% year-over-year increase, as all 23 tracked sectors saw double digit growth compared to last year.

Europe recorded the sharpest regional rise at 39% year over year, while Africa faced the highest volume at 3,834 weekly attacks per organization.

One in every 35 enterprise GenAI prompts posed a high risk of sensitive data leakage, affecting 90% of organizations that regularly use GenAI tools.

One in every 128 emails was classified as phishing, down from 1 in 91 in September; 79% of phishing emails contained links.

A total of 1,063 ransomware attacks were reported, the highest in recent years, and 35% more than in October 2025.

New n0n extortion group enters top 3 within a month after initial operation, relying heavily on AI-assisted tooling

October’s data shows a more mixed picture. Weekly attack volumes eased from September and phishing became less frequent, but attacks remain one third higher than a year ago, high-risk GenAI prompts continued to rise, and ransomware reached a record 1,063 reported attacks, with a new actor entering the top three. Together, these findings reinforce Check Point’s prevention-first view: organizations need AI-powered security, consistent visibility and shared intelligence across the full attack surface to reduce risk before it becomes business impact.

Global Cyber Attacks Ease from September but Stay Well Above Last Year

Organizations experienced an average of 2,550 cyber attacks per week in October 2026. That represents a 9% decrease from September, but still a 32% increase compared to October 2025. The monthly dip should not be read as a change in direction: attack levels remain roughly a third higher than a year ago, making resilience, exposure reduction and prevention increasingly important across networks, cloud, endpoints, email and AI services.

Education Still Faces the Highest Attack Volume While Agriculture Surges

Education remained the most targeted industry in October, averaging 5,934 weekly attacks per organization, up 33% year over year. The sector continues to face far more attacks than any other, likely reflecting the broad user base and open digital environments of schools, universities and research institutions.

Agriculture ranked second with 3,218 weekly attacks per organization, a 93% increase year over year, closely followed by Telecommunications with 3,068, up 19%. Notably, all tracked sectors recorded a double digit growth from last year, with several highly critical sectors such as Government, Energy & Utilities and Healthcare & Medical also placing in the top half of the ranking. These figures show sustained pressure on sectors with broad user bases, essential services and complex digital environments.

Africa Leads in Volume as Europe Records the Sharpest Increase

Africa recorded the highest regional attack volume in October and climbed back to top place for the first time since September 2025, averaging 3,834 weekly attacks per organization, up 38% year over year. Latin America ranked second at 3,483 weekly attacks, followed by APAC at 3,436. Europe experienced the highest rate of growth, with attacks increasing 39% compared to October 2025. North America also rose sharply, up 33% year over year. Although Europe’s overall volume remains lower than that of the leading regions, it recorded the fastest growth of any region, signaling an intensifying threat environment for organizations there.

GenAI Risk Keeps Rising

In October, 1 in every 35 enterprise GenAI prompts posed a high risk of sensitive data leakage, affecting 90% of organizations that regularly use GenAI tools. A further 12% of prompts contained potentially sensitive information, keeping data exposure a mainstream governance concern. The global high-risk rate has risen steadily, from 2.3% (1 in 43) in August to 2.5% (1 in 39) in September and 2.9% (1 in 35) in October. The average user generated 91 prompts during the month, and each organization used an average of seven tools. With the risk of data leakage via prompts on the rise, it is increasingly important to understand what employees share, where it is processed and which controls apply.

Latin America recorded the highest regional rate of high-risk prompts at 1 in 26 (3.8%), above the global average. North America followed at 1 in 30 (3.3%) and APAC at 1 in 40 (2.5%). These sectors routinely handle client, financial, citizen and patient information, which helps explain their greater exposure.

Sensitive Data Exposure Spans Core Business Information

Financial Data was the most common sensitive-data category, observed in GenAI prompts at 71% of organizations. Legal and Regulatory data and Network and IT Infrastructure followed at 70% each, Employee and HR data at 67%, and personally identifiable information at 62%. These percentages reflect the share of organizations where each category was observed, not the share of prompts. Network and IT Infrastructure information, such as hardware and network configurations and IP addresses, could give attackers valuable insight into an organization’s internal environment if exposed.

North America was the most affected region, accounting for 48% of reported ransomware incidents, followed by Europe at 22% and APAC at 18%. The United States accounted for 44.3% of reported victims, substantially ahead of Germany at 5.2% and Canada at 4.0%. These figures show where publicly claimed victims are concentrated, rather than the level of risk faced by an individual organization in each country.

The Gentlemen Leads the Ransomware Rankings as n0n Enters the Top Three

The Gentlemen was the most prevalent ransomware group in October, responsible for 13% of published attacks. Qilin followed with 12%, while n0n accounted for 8%, entering the top three only one month after appearing for the first time, and quadrupling its monthly share of published victims. The number of active groups has remained stable over the past three months, as new groups became active while others did not show continuous operations.

The Gentlemen: A fast-growing Ransomware-as-a-Service operation founded in mid-2025. It operates as both a RaaS provider and an Initial Access Broker, offering affiliates access to approximately 14,000 pre-exploited FortiGate devices, and supports Windows, Linux and ESXi environments.

Qilin: An established Ransomware-as-a-Service group with victim disclosures dating back to 2022. It provides affiliates with encryption, negotiation and support infrastructure, and has significantly increased its victim listings since March 2025.

n0n: A data-theft and extortion operation that emerged in September 2026 and had claimed more than 170 victims by early November. Its operators made extensive use of AI-assisted tooling, and initial access in observed cases relied on weak or stolen credentials rather than exploited vulnerabilities.

What October Tells Us

October’s figures show the average cyber risk easing month over month but remaining high year over year. Weekly attacks per organization fell 9% from September, and phishing became less frequent, yet attack rates are up in every region and industry compared with last year, high-risk GenAI prompts exposing organizations to data leakage continued to rise, and ransomware remained well above last year’s level and reached a new all time high. The quick rise of n0n, whose operators relied heavily on commercial generative-AI platforms, illustrates how adoption of AI tools accelerates and amplifies the operations and threats posed by attackers.

Organizations should focus on reducing exposure early, before attackers can act on it. Check Point’s prevention-first approach brings together AI-powered protection, shared intelligence and consistent governance across hybrid networks, cloud environments, digital workspaces and AI systems. As established and emerging risks converge, a unified security architecture can help teams prevent threats earlier, reduce complexity and secure AI adoption with greater confidence.

articles.title: From Water Systems to Supermarket Refrigerators: Inside Shahid Kaveh and CyberAv3ngers’ OT Attacks
articles.context: A Timeline of CyberAv3ngers and Shahid Kaveh Activity 2023: CyberAv3ngers targets water infrastructure In 2023, Check Point Research documented CyberAv3ngers activity following...
articles.full_text:
What does a cyberattack on hundreds of supermarket refrigerators in France have to do with attacks on American water systems? More than you might think.

France has attributed the October sabotage of refrigeration systems at around 700 retail sites to Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Center of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Attackers manipulated refrigeration controllers, triggering abnormal defrost cycles and disabling temperature alerts. The incidents caused widespread food losses and, according to French authorities, fires at several locations.

The name Shahid Kaveh may be new to many. Its activity is much more familiar.

CyberAv3ngers is one of the public-facing personas associated with the Shahid Kaveh unit, according to the recent French attribution. Check Point Research has been following CyberAv3ngers activity for years, particularly its interest in operational technology (OT) and industrial control systems. The latest events in France put that history into a new context.

A Timeline of CyberAv3ngers and Shahid Kaveh Activity

2023: CyberAv3ngers targets water infrastructure

In 2023, Check Point Research documented CyberAv3ngers activity following attacks against critical infrastructure in the United States.

The group targeted Unitronics programmable logic controllers used by organizations including water utilities. Our research highlighted how CyberAv3ngers was expanding beyond its traditional focus on Israel and increasingly claiming attacks against organizations in the United States, often framing Israeli-made technology itself as a target.

Following this activity, CISA and other U.S. authorities published an advisory detailing IRGC-affiliated cyber activity targeting Unitronics programmable logic controllers across multiple U.S. organizations, including water and wastewater facilities.

There was another important characteristic to this activity. Check Point Research observed Iranian-affiliated hacktivist groups combining genuine attacks with recycled, exaggerated and potentially false claims. This made separating the technical activity from the information operation surrounding it increasingly important.

March 2026: Attention turns again to exposed industrial systems

During Epic Fury in March 2026, Check Point Research continued tracking activity associated with CyberAvengers.

Our researchers identified scanning activity targeting internet-exposed Virtual Network Computing (VNC) services at Israeli industrial facilities. The scanning originated from virtual private server infrastructure associated with CyberAv3ngers, providing another indication of the group’s continued interest in exposed technology within industrial environments.

The activity reinforced a pattern researchers had already seen: internet-exposed technology used in industrial environments can give attackers opportunities to identify and potentially reach systems responsible for physical processes.

October 2026: Refrigeration systems across France are attacked

Then came France.

During the night of October 11 to 12, attackers compromised refrigeration controllers across around 700 French retail sites. According to the French investigation, the attackers remotely manipulated Danfoss and Dixell refrigeration controllers, raised defrost settings and disabled temperature safety alerts.

The consequences moved quickly beyond the digital world. Retailers lost large quantities of perishable food, with French authorities estimating losses in the tens of millions of euros, while fires were reported at multiple locations.

France attributed the destructive activity to Shahid Kaveh, identifying CyberAveng3rs among its public-facing personas.

Why Operational Technology Is an Important Part of the Story

Taken together, these incidents illustrate why attacks against operational technology deserve particular attention.

We are not only talking about computers, emails or corporate networks. Connected technology increasingly controls processes in the physical world: refrigeration, water treatment, manufacturing equipment, energy systems and other industrial operations. That changes the potential impact of a cyberattack.

In the incidents documented by Check Point Research in 2023, CyberAv3ngers targeted programmable controllers used in critical infrastructure. In France, the latest attributed activity affected the technology responsible for maintaining refrigeration temperatures.

Different systems, different incidents, but a common lesson: when operational technology is exposed to the internet, a cyber intrusion can potentially translate into physical disruption.

From CyberAv3ngers to Shahid Kaveh

The French attribution also helps put years of activity under CyberAv3ngers into a wider organizational context. Check Point Research’s earlier analysis identified CyberAv3ngers as an Iranian government and IRGC-affiliated public facing persona. For defenders, the name matters less than the behavior behind it. The progression from attacks on water infrastructure to reconnaissance of industrial systems and now disruptive activity against refrigeration infrastructure shows why exposed OT environments remain an important area to monitor.

As geopolitical tensions evolve, Check Point Research will continue tracking Iranian cyber activity and the infrastructure, techniques and personas associated with it.

Follow Check Point Research for the latest insights into Iranian cyber activity and emerging threats.

articles.title: What 70 European CISOs told us about securing the AI era
articles.context: Prevention has become more urgent AI has shrunk the time between a vulnerability being found and being exploited
articles.full_text:
Last week I spent three days in Bavaria with more than 70 CISOs from across Europe, the Middle East and Africa at Leaders Point EMEA. Led by our CEO Nadav Zafrir and hosted with Team8’s CISO Village, it was our second Leaders Point and the first in Europe. We kept it invitation-only so people could speak openly.

The timing was hard to miss. Over the past month, attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems have spoiled food and emptied shelves in stores across France and several other European countries. Nobody has yet been shown to be behind them. For anyone who still sees cyber risk as an IT problem, it was a sharp reminder of how physical it has become.

As Nadav told the room, our industry is going through its most dramatic shift in 30 years. CISOs now have three jobs at once: protect their organizations from AI-driven threats, secure the AI their own teams use, and apply AI in their own defense. They are doing all of this while the rules are still being written.

We host Leaders Point to listen, because Check Point’s strategy depends on seeing these challenges from our customers’ point of view. We covered a lot of ground, from a CISO panel on “Whose AI Can Europe Trust?” to national cyber leadership in the AI era and a look inside the frontier AI labs. Four themes kept coming back.

Prevention has become more urgent

AI has shrunk the time between a vulnerability being found and being exploited. Attackers can use AI to find weaknesses and turn them into working attacks far faster than before. Patching faster on its own can no longer keep up.

The CISOs I spoke to are rethinking what prevention means. They want to harden their environments and remove whole classes of risk before an attack arrives, so that each new vulnerability matters less. Prevention has been at the heart of Check Point’s approach for a long time, and it was powerful to hear the same conclusion from the people running security every day.

The supermarket attacks show why. Reporting on them points to refrigeration controllers that could be reached from the open internet, many on software their maker no longer updated. No patch was ever coming for those systems. The only real defense was to close those doors before anyone went looking.

AI agents need controls built around their purpose

AI agents now act with legitimate credentials across email, endpoints, networks and the cloud. That makes them hard to police with traditional tools. To most systems, an agent doing something harmful looks the same as an agent doing its job.

The room kept coming back to purpose. To secure an agent, you need to know what it is supposed to do and check every action it takes against that, in real time. An agent built to summarize contracts has no reason to change firewall rules, and security teams need to be able to see and stop that the moment it happens.

There has been plenty of talk lately about kill switches for AI agents. You should have one: if an agent is hijacked, you pull the plug. But most risky agents aren’t malicious. They’re just determined, and take a dangerous shortcut to finish the job. Switch that agent off and you lose the work too. The kill switch is the last resort. Steering is the first move: catch the agent drifting toward danger, stop the risky step and keep the work going. If stopping agents is your whole strategy, you don’t have an agent strategy. You have an off switch.

Every AI use case needs a human owner

As AI makes more decisions and takes more actions, it becomes easy for the outcomes to end up as nobody’s responsibility. The CISOs were clear that this can’t be allowed to happen.

Every AI use case needs a named owner who signs off on its risk, the same way they would for any other business risk. Clear ownership is what lets organizations move quickly with AI and still know who answers when something goes wrong.

European organizations want control over their AI choices

Many conversations, including our panel on whose AI Europe can trust, came back to control. European organizations want the freedom to switch AI models and suppliers as the market changes, and to build independent capability where it matters most.

For CISOs this is a practical question of resilience. Relying on a single model or provider is a concentration risk like any other. Our job is to secure AI whichever models and suppliers our customers choose.

The decisions that matter will be made this year

By this time next year, many of the decisions that define how organizations secure AI will have been made. The leaders in that room in Bavaria will make a lot of them.

I’m grateful to every CISO who gave us three days of their time and their candor, and to Team8’s CISO Village for building Leaders Point with us. What we heard will shape what Check Point builds next, and we’ll keep listening.

articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Meta FAIRChem
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Meta FAIRChem. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of checkpoint files. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.
